First love, growing up · 2011

You Are the Apple of My EyeMischief and Unequal Memory

Marina reviews Giddens Ko’s Taiwanese coming-of-age romance, finding lively performances and tender detail alongside its narrow view of first love.

By MarinaOctober 17, 20263 min readSpoiler-light review

In this review

A Romance Built from Motion and MischiefWhose Memory Gets to Define the Romance?Sources & references
Film
You Are the Apple of My Eye
Director
Giddens Ko
Year
2011

Giddens Ko’s You Are the Apple of My Eye begins with a familiar arrangement: a restless boy, a disciplined girl, and a classroom full of friends who turn attraction into a competition. Set largely around a Taiwanese high school in the 1990s, it follows Ko Ching-teng as he is pushed toward Shen Chia-yi, the model student he pretends not to admire. What makes the film inviting is not the novelty of this setup, but the way its teasing, dares, and small acts of defiance make adolescence feel immediate without treating it as sacred.

A Romance Built from Motion and Mischief

The film’s strongest quality is its sense of motion. Ko cuts between boisterous group comedy, awkward study sessions, schoolyard challenges, and quieter stretches in which a glance or a half-finished sentence changes the temperature of a scene. The soundtrack and period details give the story a lived-in rhythm: phones are less convenient, time is more public, and friendship occupies nearly every available space. These details do more than decorate the past; they show how romance grows inside a community before it becomes a private feeling.

Ko Chen-tung plays Ching-teng as an appealing nuisance, someone whose confidence is often just impatience wearing a grin. His comic timing keeps the character watchable even when his immaturity becomes difficult to excuse. Michelle Chen brings a different kind of force to Chia-yi: her composure is not blank sweetness, but an active intelligence that quietly manages the boys around her. Their chemistry works because the film lets attraction emerge through friction, correction, and competition rather than polished declarations.

I also appreciate how the film allows male friendship to remain central instead of using the friends as disposable comic scenery. Their vulgar jokes and elaborate schemes can be exhausting, yet they create a believable social world in which tenderness is disguised as mockery. The humor has a deliberately uneven edge, moving from charmingly juvenile to needlessly crude. That imbalance is a real limitation: the film sometimes asks us to accept behavior as lovable simply because it belongs to a nostalgic memory.

Whose Memory Gets to Define the Romance?

The larger problem is that the story remains closely tied to Ching-teng’s perspective. Chia-yi is vivid in performance, but the writing gives us fewer chances to inhabit her uncertainty, desires, or private logic. The film knows this imbalance exists and occasionally turns Ching-teng’s self-importance against him, which lends the romance a welcome honesty. Still, its emotional architecture is more interested in what he learns than in what she might be withholding, and that makes the relationship feel less mutual than its best scenes suggest.

What stays with me is the film’s understanding that growing up is not a clean exchange of lessons. People can be sincere and selfish in the same moment; a joke can protect a feeling while also hurting someone. You Are the Apple of My Eye is most persuasive when it trusts those contradictions, especially in the pauses after the laughter has passed. It is less convincing when it leans on familiar nostalgia, but its lively performances and attentive sense of youthful time give the romance a pulse that is difficult to dismiss.
